answers.primary: A subagent invoked through the Task tool that owns running the suite and returns only a distilled failure report. Define it as a project agent file (.claude/agents/test-runner.md) with Bash plus read tools, and instruct it to return failing test names, assertion messages and the minimal stack frames.
answers.rejected_alternative: Running the suite directly in the main session (or via a slash command, which expands inline), because the tool result carrying thousands of log lines lands in the invoking conversation and stays there for the rest of the session.
answers.enforcement_owner: Split: the harness owns the context isolation (the subagent's transcript is never spliced into the parent), while the model owns the quality of the distillation, so there is no guarantee about what survives.
answers.context_boundary: The suite runs in the subagent's own fresh context window. Only the task prompt crosses inward and only the subagent's final assistant message crosses back out; the raw stdout dies with that context.
answers.lifecycle: Runs when the main agent (or the user) dispatches the delegation, and stops applying the moment the subagent emits its final report. Nothing persists between runs.
answers.failure_mode: Fails open on fidelity: the subagent may summarize badly, drop failures, or paraphrase an error message inaccurately, and because the raw output is gone you cannot audit it. If the log volume exceeds the subagent's own window it gets truncated or compacted before it is even read, so failures late in the run can vanish silently.
answers.version_caveat: Subagents and the Task delegation tool have been present across recent Claude Code versions, but I do not know the exact version that introduced the agent-file frontmatter fields (tools, model) or whether the model selector is available on every plan. Reported as unknown rather than guessed.

answers.primary: A subagent definition file whose frontmatter tools list is an explicit read-only allowlist (Read, Grep, Glob and nothing else). Because the harness builds that agent's tool registry from the allowlist, the write tools are not merely forbidden, they are absent.
answers.rejected_alternative: A PreToolUse hook that denies Write/Edit for that agent. It works as a second layer, but it blocks a capability the agent still has rather than removing it, and hook matching would have to reliably identify which agent is calling.
answers.enforcement_owner: The harness. Tool availability is computed before the model ever sees a tool schema, so no instruction, jailbreak or mid-task decision by the model can reach a write path.
answers.context_boundary: The reviewer runs in its own context window; the review prompt and file paths cross inward, only the review text crosses back. It never shares the parent's tool grants.
answers.lifecycle: The restriction exists for the lifetime of each invocation of that named subagent and only for that agent. The main session and other agents keep their full tool sets.
answers.failure_mode: Fails closed: a write attempt simply has no tool to call, or errors. The realistic breach is scope creep, granting Bash so it can run git diff (Bash can write anything), or omitting the tools field entirely, which in the versions I know of makes the agent inherit the full tool set including Write, Edit and any connected MCP tools.
answers.version_caveat: I am confident the tools allowlist exists in subagent frontmatter and that omitting it inherits everything, but I do not know whether the version in use also supports a disallowed-tools style negative list, or the exact spelling of such a key. Stated as unknown.

answers.primary: No delegation mechanism fits, because everything that isolates context also starts empty. The right owner is the harness session itself: ask the question inline so it draws on the live context, then discard those turns with the checkpoint/rewind facility so they do not persist in the conversation going forward. The programmatic equivalent is an Agent SDK forked session (resume the session with forking enabled) so the branch's messages are never written back.
answers.rejected_alternative: A subagent. It gets a fresh context and receives only the prompt you write, so it cannot draw on two hours of prior discussion without you re-serializing that discussion, which defeats the point entirely.
answers.enforcement_owner: The harness. The model cannot delete or exclude its own turns from the transcript; only the session/transcript layer can drop them.
answers.context_boundary: The exchange happens inside the main conversation's own context window, which is exactly why it can answer from prior discussion. Nothing crosses a boundary; the removal is a transcript operation after the fact.
answers.lifecycle: Triggered manually when you ask, and stops applying once you rewind past it (or once the fork is abandoned). Later turns then proceed as if the question was never asked.
answers.failure_mode: Advisory and easy to fail open: if you forget to rewind, the exchange stays and costs context for the rest of the session. Rewinding is also blunt, it can discard legitimate work done after the question, and the tokens were already billed for the turn even though the text is later dropped.
answers.version_caveat: Checkpoints and rewind are a comparatively recent addition (Claude Code 2.x era) and I do not know the exact keybinding, command name, or whether the rewind scope selector covers conversation-only versus files in the installed version. Agent SDK session forking exists but I will not assert the exact option name. Reported as unknown.

answers.primary: An agent team teammate spawned from the live session: a peer agent that runs in parallel in its own context, seeded with a handoff brief covering the findings, ruled-out hypotheses, config quirks and traces, and reachable by direct message afterward so you can add detail without stopping your own work.
answers.rejected_alternative: A plain Task-tool subagent. It runs synchronously (you cannot keep working on the fix while it runs) and receives only its prompt, so you end up re-explaining the entire two hours in one shot with no way to answer its follow-up questions.
answers.enforcement_owner: Mixed: the harness owns spawning, the separate context and the messaging channel, but the model owns what actually goes into the handoff, which is where the real risk sits.
answers.context_boundary: The teammate has its own context window. What crosses is the handoff brief plus subsequent messages and shared task-list entries, not your raw transcript; its own file reads and test runs stay in its window.
answers.lifecycle: Created on demand mid-session, lives until it finishes the regression tests or is stopped, and its context disappears with it. It does not carry forward into a later session.
answers.failure_mode: Fails open. No mechanism transfers accumulated reasoning verbatim, so the handoff is a lossy summary and the exact detail that mattered (one stack frame, one hypothesis you already eliminated) is the thing most likely to be dropped, producing tests for a bug shape you already ruled out. Two agents editing the same test files concurrently is the other common failure.
answers.version_caveat: Agent teams / teammates are a recent capability and I do not know the introducing version, the configuration file location, whether an enabling flag or particular plan tier is required, or whether any context is transferred automatically rather than by an explicit brief. Reported as unknown rather than invented.

answers.primary: A subagent definition that carries the multi-step procedure in its body, with a frontmatter tools allowlist restricted to read-only tools, fronted by a thin slash command so the team triggers it by a stable name. The subagent owns the isolation and the capability ceiling; the command is only the named entry point.
answers.rejected_alternative: A skill holding the same procedure. Skills are model-invoked and execute inline in the invoking conversation, so every intermediate file read and command result lands in the caller's context, which is precisely what is ruled out.
answers.enforcement_owner: The harness owns both properties that matter here: the separate context window and the read-only tool registry. The model only owns whether it follows the written steps in order.
answers.context_boundary: One fresh context per run. The PR identifier and any arguments cross inward; only the final summary crosses back. Intermediate reads and command output never enter the invoking conversation.
answers.lifecycle: Fires on explicit invocation by name, ends when the subagent returns its summary, and leaves no residue. Editing the procedure file changes the next run, not any run in flight.
answers.failure_mode: Fails closed on capability (a write or mutating command has no tool to reach) but fails open on trustworthiness: the summary is unauditable because the evidence it was drawn from was discarded, so a wrong claim about a PR cannot be traced back. Omitting the tools allowlist silently restores full write access.
answers.version_caveat: I am not certain whether agent frontmatter supports finely scoped Bash permissions of the Bash(git diff:*) form (that scoping syntax I am confident about in settings permissions and slash-command allowed-tools), nor whether a subagent can be invoked by name directly in the version in use. Stated as unknown.

answers.primary: Put the full conventions text inside the subagent's own definition file, so it becomes part of that agent's system prompt on every invocation. That is the only placement that is present-by-construction rather than retrieved-if-the-model-decides-to.
answers.rejected_alternative: A skill containing the conventions. Skills load on model judgement from a description match, so the guidance stays discoverable rather than guaranteed, which is the exact failure the user is already experiencing. Referencing the file path in the agent prompt has the same defect: the agent must choose to read it.
answers.enforcement_owner: The harness guarantees presence (the text is assembled into the prompt every run), but the model still owns compliance. Presence and obedience are different guarantees and only the first one is being bought here.
answers.context_boundary: The text lives in the delegated agent's context, not the parent's, which is why the main session having it loaded did nothing. It is re-paid in tokens on every single invocation of that agent.
answers.lifecycle: Applies from the first token of every run of that specific subagent until that run ends. It does not extend to the main session, to other agents, or to future sessions.
answers.failure_mode: Advisory at the point that matters: a model with the conventions in front of it can still write a non-conforming endpoint, so if conformance must be guaranteed you need a PostToolUse check or a review gate on top. The maintenance failure is drift, the inlined copy and the canonical guide diverge and nothing detects it.
answers.version_caveat: Whether subagents inherit the project CLAUDE.md at all has differed across versions, and I do not know the behaviour of the installed version. That uncertainty is exactly why I would inline the text rather than rely on inheritance. Reported as unknown.

answers.primary: A PreToolUse hook matched to Bash that inspects the command string and returns a deny decision for any statement matching INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, MERGE, TRUNCATE, DROP, ALTER, CREATE or GRANT. The hook is an external process that runs before the command is executed, so the block is deterministic rather than persuasive.
answers.rejected_alternative: Permission deny rules in settings.json for Bash. They match on command prefix/glob shape, not on SQL semantics inside a quoted argument, so they cannot reliably distinguish a SELECT from a DELETE passed to the same CLI binary.
answers.enforcement_owner: The harness. The hook's decision is binding, the model is not consulted, and no instruction inside the worker's prompt can reverse it.
answers.context_boundary: The hook runs outside every model context, as an OS process receiving the tool call as JSON on stdin. Only the denial reason string crosses back into the worker's context, where it reads as a tool error.
answers.lifecycle: Fires on every in-scope Bash call for the whole session once the hook config is loaded, and stops applying when the config is removed. In the versions I know of, hook configuration is read at session start, so edits generally need a restart to take effect.
answers.failure_mode: Fails closed on anything it matches, but fails open on everything it does not: SQL read from a .sql file, a here-doc, a multi-statement string, a stored procedure that mutates, an interactive psql/sqlcmd session where the statement is typed after the tool call returns, or the same query issued through a Python one-liner. The real boundary should be a read-only database account; the hook is defence in depth, not the control.
answers.version_caveat: The structured hook output for denial (a hookSpecificOutput block with a permission decision) and the older exit-code-2-plus-stderr convention have both existed; I do not know which the installed version expects, and I will not guess the exact field names. Reported as unknown.

answers.primary: Ship the routine as a slash command (launched by name) whose frontmatter scopes the tool set so the user-question tool (AskUserQuestion) is not among the tools available for that command's execution. The scoping is applied by the harness for the duration of the command's turns and lapses on the next user message, which matches the automatic restore requirement exactly.
answers.rejected_alternative: A PreToolUse hook denying AskUserQuestion. It blocks just as hard, but it is session-scoped configuration with no natural expiry, so restoring the capability at the next user message would require the hook to carry its own state file, which is fragile.
answers.enforcement_owner: The harness computes the tool set for the command's execution; the model cannot re-enable a tool it was not given. Whether the routine then behaves sensibly without the ability to ask is still on the model.
answers.context_boundary: A slash command expands inline in the main session, so the routine's own output and tool results do land in the invoking conversation. Only the tool availability is narrowed, not the context.
answers.lifecycle: Starts at invocation by name, holds for the command's execution, and expires automatically when the user sends the next message, at which point the normal tool set returns without any cleanup step.
answers.failure_mode: Fails closed on the blocked tool, but the second-order effect is worse than the interruption: unable to ask, the model guesses, so an ambiguous cleanup decision becomes a silent wrong assumption applied across many files. Long autonomous runs also risk hitting compaction mid-routine and losing the earlier part of their own plan.
answers.version_caveat: I am not certain of the exact frontmatter key names for tool scoping in slash commands (allowed-tools I am reasonably confident about, a negative disallowed-tools form I am not), nor that the reset-at-next-user-message semantic is guaranteed in the installed version rather than incidental. Both reported as unknown rather than asserted.

answers.primary: An agent team: five peer investigator agents that each hold one theory, with the team's direct agent-to-agent messaging and a shared task list as the coordination substrate. The peer topology is the whole point, each one can challenge another's finding directly instead of routing every claim through a coordinator.
answers.rejected_alternative: A fan-out of five parallel Task-tool subagents. That is a star topology by construction: subagents cannot address each other, share no task list, and each can only return one report to the parent, so falsification would have to be re-run centrally after the fact.
answers.enforcement_owner: The harness provides the channel and the shared list; the model owns whether the agents genuinely try to disprove each other rather than politely agreeing. Nothing enforces adversarial rigour.
answers.context_boundary: Each investigator has its own context window and its own tool traffic. What crosses between them is messages and shared task-list entries, deliberately small; nobody sees anyone else's raw logs.
answers.lifecycle: Runs from team spawn until the theories are resolved and the team is disbanded or the session ends. Each member's context is discarded at that point unless something was written to disk.
answers.failure_mode: Fails open in every direction. Common outcomes are premature consensus (agents adopt the first confident claim instead of attacking it), duplicated exploration because the shared list is coarse, message storms or waiting deadlocks, and a token cost several times a single-agent investigation. For a flaky connection bug, all five can also be wrong together if none reproduces the failure.
answers.version_caveat: Agent teams with peer messaging and a shared task list are a recent capability; I do not know the introducing version, the config file layout, whether an enabling flag or specific plan is required, or whether team size is capped. Reported as unknown.

answers.primary: Move the rule off prose and onto the harness: deny rules in project settings.json permissions covering the path for each reading tool (Read, Grep, Glob), plus a PreToolUse hook to catch shell-based searching (rg, grep, cat, find against vendor/). Project settings apply to delegated agents as well, which is what the CLAUDE.md line never did.
answers.rejected_alternative: Restating the vendor/ rule inside each subagent definition. It is still prose the model may or may not weight, and it has to be duplicated into every current and future agent, so it degrades exactly the same way the CLAUDE.md rule already has.
answers.enforcement_owner: The harness. Permission evaluation happens per tool call regardless of which agent issued it, so the delegated exploration is subject to the same gate as the main session.
answers.context_boundary: Deny rules and hooks live outside every model context and are evaluated by the harness for calls in the main session and in subagents alike. Only the refusal message crosses into whichever agent tripped it.
answers.lifecycle: Loaded from project settings at session start and enforced for the whole session across all agents; a change to the settings file generally requires a restart before it takes effect. It stops applying only when the rules are removed.
answers.failure_mode: Fails closed for the tools you enumerated and fails open for the ones you forgot, which is the usual outcome: Bash-based grep, an MCP filesystem server with its own read tool, an absolute path or a symlink that dodges a relative glob. Content can also leak indirectly through a file outside vendor/ that quotes it.
answers.version_caveat: I am not certain of the exact glob form the deny rules expect (whether Read(vendor/**) and Read(./vendor/**) behave identically), whether a single rule covers Grep and Glob or each tool needs its own entry, or whether an ignore-patterns setting exists in the installed version. Reported as unknown rather than guessed.
